newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada to pursue Asia, Latin America markets.
newsitem.headline: Canada to pursue Asia, Latin America markets.

text.p: Canada's newly re-elected Liberal government hopes to boost trade with Asia Pacific countries and Latin America in its second term, Trade Minister Art Eggleton said on Wednesday.

"At the moment, the priority is toward regional agreements," especially with the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation forum and the Free Trade of the Americas Agreement, which are currently being hammered out, Eggleton told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Eggleton was trade minister in the last Liberal government. The Liberals won a reduced majority in Canada's election on Monday. Eggleton said he hoped to retain his post.
"I hope to be in the cabinet and I'd love to have this (portfolio) once again," he said.
Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Wednesday that he would swear in the new cabinet in exactly one week.
Eggleton said he also hoped to step up talks with South American free trade block Mercosur in hopes of increasing Canada's exports and investment to Mercosur countries.
About 85 percent of Canada's exports go the United States.
Eggleton said he wanted more small and medium-sized businesses involed in trade, to double the number of Canadian exporters by the year 2000.
As for recurring squabbles with the United States over lumber, grain and cultural exports, Eggleton said he would stay the course.

Canada and the United States have just begun the second year of a five-year quota agreement on lumber that penalizes Canadian companies if they export more than 14.7 million board feet of lumber a year.
Eggleton said he hoped to return to a free market system after the agreement ended and that he detected some U.S. flexibility.

"I think what we're beginning to see here in the U.S. is a bit of recognition from some other quarters other than the mill operators," he said. "They're all feeling the high prices" that have stemmed from the quota system.
He said he had a standing request with the United States to relax the quota level, but had not had much of a response.
With grain, Eggleton said he would continue to resist U.S. pressure to cap Canadian exports.
He added he would continue to defend protection of Canadian cultural industries, although he said the means of protection might have to change.
"I expect culture is still going to be an issue," he said.
